description: Phase 2 A/B set: bloated prompts that fire the rewrite gate, with deterministic checks. Rewrite stays OFF unless arm B beats arm A on this set.

items.prompt: So basically what I am trying to get at, and I apologise in advance because I know I am rambling quite a lot here and probably repeating myself several times over, but what I really truly want to understand at the end of the day, when all is said and done, is the concept that people in the world of computing and specifically in the world of artificial intelligence and large language models keep referring to over and over again, namely the idea of quote unquote time to first token, sometimes abbreviated as TTFT, and I would really appreciate it if you could explain to me in plain simple English that anybody could understand what exactly this term means, why it matters at all, and whether it has anything to do with how responsive a chat application feels to the person using it, because I have heard people say it does but I am not sure I believe them, and while I am on the subject let me give you a whole lot of context you almost certainly do not need, because context is king as my old manager used to say, back when I worked at a company that shall remain nameless where we spent most of our time in meetings about meetings, and in one of those meetings somebody put up a slide, and I remember this vividly because the slide had a pie chart on it that made no sense whatsoever, and on that slide it said something about latency budgets and user perception thresholds and how anything over some number of milliseconds feels sluggish to a human being, and everyone nodded sagely including me even though at the time I had absolutely no idea what any of it meant, and ever since that day I have been meaning to sit down and actually get my head around this stuff properly, because I now find myself in a position where I am evaluating chat applications for my own team, lovely bunch of people by the way, very patient with me, and the vendors keep throwing these terms around in their sales decks, TTFT this and tokens per second that and streaming latency the other, and I nod along just like I did in that meeting all those years ago, which frankly is a habit I am trying to break, so here we are, this is me breaking the habit, asking the question I should have asked a long time ago, and to be crystal clear about what I am actually asking, because I am aware I have gone on a very long walk to get here: please explain what time to first token means, why it matters, and how it relates to how responsive a chat application feels, and please keep your answer reasonably short, ideally just a few sentences, definitely under two thousand characters in total.

Right, so, here is the thing, and again forgive the extremely long-winded way I am going about asking what is fundamentally an extremely simple question, but I have a spreadsheet, well actually it is not really a spreadsheet, it is more of a mental model of a spreadsheet if you will, and before I get to the numbers let me explain why I even have this mental spreadsheet in the first place, because I think the background is illuminating even if it is not strictly relevant, you see every quarter my business partner and I sit down over coffee, always the same cafe, always the same corner table, and we go through what we grandly call our financial review, which in practice means me scribbling numbers on a napkin while my partner questions every single one of them, and this quarter the napkin got thrown away by an overzealous waiter before I could transcribe it, true story, so now I am reconstructing the figures from memory, which brings me to the actual numbers, and in this notional spreadsheet of mine there are two numbers that matter for the purposes of this conversation, the first number being one hundred and twenty five, which represents revenue in thousands of dollars, and I am quite confident about that one because it was circled twice on the napkin, and the second number being seventy five, which represents costs, also in thousands of dollars, slightly less confident about that one but let us go with it, and I should mention for completeness that there were other numbers on the napkin too, depreciation figures and some speculative projections for next year and a doodle of a sailboat that my partner insists is a tax writeoff joke I do not fully understand, but none of those other numbers matter here, only the two I have given you, and I want to stress, because my partner will absolutely ask me where these figures came from and whether a computer did the sums or whether I did them myself on the back of yet another napkin, that what I am after here is the straightforward arithmetic, no rounding surprises, no currency conversions, no inflation adjustments, none of the clever stuff, just the plain honest numbers, and so what I need you to do for me, if you would be so kind, is to tell me what the gross profit is in thousands of dollars, that is to say revenue minus costs, and also what the gross margin percentage works out to be, rounded to the nearest whole percent, and nothing else, no commentary on my bookkeeping practices, no advice about napkins, keep it brief please.

Okay so bear with me here because context is everything, or so they say, and I want to give you all of it even though most of it is probably not strictly necessary for the task at hand, which as you will see in a moment is really quite trivial: I am putting together a tiny reference card for my team, we are a small team, lovely people, five of us in total counting the intern who started last month and who to be perfectly honest already knows more about this stuff than I do, which is precisely why I want the reference card to be immaculate, because nothing undermines your authority as a team lead quite like handing out a cheat sheet with a mistake on it, I learned that lesson the hard way with a git commands poster that had the arguments to rebase backwards, the intern spotted it within about eleven seconds and I have never fully recovered my standing, anyway, the card, the card is part of a little onboarding pack I am assembling, there is a page about our coding standards, a page about how we do code review, a page with the wifi password which I am told is a security risk but that is a battle for another day, and then this page, the one you are helping me with, and this page is about the classic HTTP methods used in REST APIs, you know the ones, the verbs that every web developer uses every single day of their working life, and I did consider just writing them down from memory but see above regarding the rebase poster incident, once bitten twice shy as they say, so I am outsourcing my confidence to you, and I know what you are thinking, you are thinking this fellow could have looked this up in any textbook or indeed any search engine in a fraction of the time it took him to type this message, and you would be entirely correct, but where would be the fun in that, and besides, I am testing this new chat system my company is evaluating and I was told to give it a realistic workload, and if forty years in this industry have taught me anything it is that there is nothing more realistic than a simple question wrapped in an unreasonable quantity of preamble, so, with all of that now thoroughly on the record, and with my apologies once again for the sheer length of this message, here specifically is what I want, and here at long last is the actual request, buried at the bottom of this message like the last biscuit in the tin: I want you to list exactly four of them, the four most commonly used ones for create, read, update and delete operations respectively, one per line, just the method names in capital letters, no explanations, no numbering, no punctuation, nothing fancy whatsoever, just the four method names and that is all.
In one sentence, what does a cache do?
